# snafu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snafu/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#snafu)SNAFU

SNAFU is a library to easily generate errors and add information to underlying errors, especially when the same underlying error type can occur in different contexts.

For detailed information, please see the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro and the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- [Turnkey errors based on strings](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)
- [Custom error types](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)- Including a conversion path from turnkey errors

- [Backtraces](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- Extension traits for
- [Error reporting](https://docs.rs#reporting)
- Suitable for libraries and applications
- `no_std`compatibility
- Generic types and lifetimes

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

If you want to report errors without hassle, start with the
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) type and the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)

`whatever!````
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Whatever> {
    if id < 10 {
        whatever!("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
You can also use it to wrap any other error:

```
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Whatever> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path)
        .with_whatever_context(|_| format!("Could not read file {path}"))
}
```
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) allows for a short message and tracks a

[for every error:](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)

`Backtrace````
use snafu::{prelude::*, ErrorCompat, Whatever};
if let Err(e) = returns_an_error() {
    eprintln!("An error occurred: {e}");
    if let Some(bt) = ErrorCompat::backtrace(&e) {
        eprintln!("{bt}");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-error-types)Custom error types

Many projects will hit limitations of the `Whatever` type. When
that occurs, it’s time to create your own error type by deriving
[ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)!

[§](https://docs.rs#struct-style)Struct style

SNAFU will read your error struct definition and create a *context
selector* type (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this example). These
context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html) macro to provide
ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
struct InvalidIdError {
    id: u16,
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), InvalidIdError> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to your error, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#enum-style)Enum style

While error structs are good for constrained cases, they don’t allow for reporting multiple possible kinds of errors at one time. Error enums solve that problem.

SNAFU will read your error enum definition and create a *context
selector* type for each variant (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this
example). These context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
macro to provide ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to a variant, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
    ConfigFile {
        source: std::io::Error,
        path: String,
    },
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Error> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
You can combine the power of the [ whatever!](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html) macro with an
enum error type. This is great if you started out with

[and are moving to a custom error type:](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)

`Whatever````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
    #[snafu(whatever, display("{message}"))]
    Whatever {
        message: String,
        #[snafu(source(from(Box<dyn std::error::Error>, Some)))]
        source: Option<Box<dyn std::error::Error>>,
    },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    whatever!("Just kidding... this function always fails!");
    Ok(())
}
```
You may wish to make the type `Send` and/or `Sync`, allowing
your error type to be used in multithreaded programs, by changing
`dyn std::error::Error` to `dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#reporting)Reporting

Printing an error via [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)
will only show the top-level error message without the underlying sources.
For an extended error report,
SNAFU offers a user-friendly error output mechanism.
It prints the main error and all underlying errors in the chain,
from the most recent to the oldest,
plus the

[backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)if applicable. This is done by using the

[procedural macro or the](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)

`report`[type directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)

`Report````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not load configuration file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
#[snafu::report]
fn main() -> Result<(), ConfigFileError> {
    read_config_file("bad-config.ini")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
This will print:

```
Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini
Caused by this error:
1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
Which shows the underlying errors, unlike [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html):

`Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini`… and is also more readable than the [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) output:

`Error: ConfigFileError { source: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }, path: "bad-config.ini" }`[§](https://docs.rs#next-steps)Next steps

Read the documentation for the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro to see all of the
capabilities, then read the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)for deeper understanding.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

way. Useful as the return type from `main`and test functions.

- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.WhateverLocal.html)- Local - `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling when the error does not need to cross a thread boundary.

- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoError.html)- Error

# SNAFU

**S**ituation **N**ormal: **A**ll **F**ouled **U**p

SNAFU is a library to easily assign underlying errors into domain-specific errors while adding context.

```
use *;

type Result<T, E = Error> = Result;
```

# backtrace - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/backtrace/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

A library for acquiring a backtrace at runtime

This library is meant to supplement the `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` support of the
standard library by allowing an acquisition of a backtrace at runtime
programmatically. The backtraces generated by this library do not need to be
parsed, for example, and expose the functionality of multiple backend
implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

First, add this to your Cargo.toml

```
[dependencies]
backtrace = "0.3"
```
Next:

```
backtrace::trace(|frame| {
    let ip = frame.ip();
    let symbol_address = frame.symbol_address();
    // Resolve this instruction pointer to a symbol name
    backtrace::resolve_frame(frame, |symbol| {
        if let Some(name) = symbol.name() {
            // ...
        }
        if let Some(filename) = symbol.filename() {
            // ...
        }
    });
    true // keep going to the next frame
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#backtrace-accuracy)Backtrace accuracy

This crate implements best-effort attempts to get the native backtrace. This is not always guaranteed to work, and some platforms don’t return any backtrace at all. If your application requires accurate backtraces then it’s recommended to closely evaluate this crate to see whether it’s suitable for your use case on your target platforms.

Even on supported platforms, there’s a number of reasons that backtraces may be less-than-accurate, including but not limited to:

-
Unwind information may not be available. This crate primarily implements backtraces by unwinding the stack, but not all functions may have unwinding information (e.g. DWARF unwinding information).
-
Rust code may be compiled without unwinding information for some functions. This can also happen for Rust code compiled with `-Cpanic=abort`. You can remedy this, however, with`-Cforce-unwind-tables`as a compiler option.
-
Unwind information may be inaccurate or corrupt. In the worst case inaccurate unwind information can lead this library to segfault. In the best case inaccurate information will result in a truncated stack trace.
-
Backtraces may not report filenames/line numbers correctly due to missing or corrupt debug information. This won’t lead to segfaults unlike corrupt unwinding information, but missing or malformed debug information will mean that filenames and line numbers will not be available. This may be because debug information wasn’t generated by the compiler, or it’s just missing on the filesystem.
-
Not all platforms are supported. For example there’s no way to get a backtrace on WebAssembly at the moment.
-
Crate features may be disabled. Currently this crate supports using Gimli libbacktrace on non-Windows platforms for reading debuginfo for backtraces. If both crate features are disabled, however, then these platforms will generate a backtrace but be unable to generate symbols for it.

In most standard workflows for most standard platforms you generally don’t need to worry about these caveats. We’ll try to fix ones where we can over time, but otherwise it’s important to be aware of the limitations of unwinding-based backtraces!

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- Representation of an owned and self-contained backtrace.
- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.BacktraceFmt.html)- Fmt
- A formatter for backtraces.
- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.BacktraceFrame.html)- Frame
- Captured version of a frame in a backtrace.
- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.BacktraceFrameFmt.html)- Frame - Fmt
- A formatter for just one frame of a backtrace.
- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.BacktraceSymbol.html)- Symbol
- Captured version of a symbol in a backtrace.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html)
- A trait representing one frame of a backtrace, yielded to the `trace`function of this crate.
- [Symbol](https://docs.rs/struct.Symbol.html)
- A trait representing the resolution of a symbol in a file.
- [Symbol](https://docs.rs/struct.SymbolName.html)- Name
- A wrapper around a symbol name to provide ergonomic accessors to the demangled name, the raw bytes, the raw string, etc.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/enum.BytesOrWideString.html)- OrWide - String
- A platform independent representation of a string. When working with `std`enabled it is recommended to the convenience methods for providing conversions to`std`types.
- [Print](https://docs.rs/enum.PrintFmt.html)- Fmt
- The styles of printing that we can print

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [clear_](https://docs.rs/fn.clear_symbol_cache.html)- symbol_ - cache
- Attempt to reclaim that cached memory used to symbolicate addresses.
- [resolve](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve.html)
- Resolve an address to a symbol, passing the symbol to the specified closure.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_frame.html)- frame
- Resolve a previously captured frame to a symbol, passing the symbol to the specified closure.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_frame_unsynchronized.html)- frame_ - unsynchronized - ⚠
- Same as `resolve_frame`, only unsafe as it’s unsynchronized.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_unsynchronized.html)- unsynchronized - ⚠
- Same as `resolve`, only unsafe as it’s unsynchronized.
- [trace](https://docs.rs/fn.trace.html)
- Inspects the current call-stack, passing all active frames into the closure provided to calculate a stack trace.
- [trace_](https://docs.rs/fn.trace_unsynchronized.html)- unsynchronized - ⚠
- Same as `trace`, only unsafe as it’s unsynchronized.

# snafu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/snafu/latest/target-redirect/snafu/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#snafu)SNAFU

SNAFU is a library to easily generate errors and add information to underlying errors, especially when the same underlying error type can occur in different contexts.

For detailed information, please see the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro and the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- [Turnkey errors based on strings](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)
- [Custom error types](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)- Including a conversion path from turnkey errors

- [Backtraces](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)

- [Error reporting](https://docs.rs#reporting)
- Suitable for libraries and applications
- `no_std`compatibility
- Generic types and lifetimes

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) type and the

```

[§](https://docs.rs#reporting)Reporting

Printing an error via [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Report````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not load configuration file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
#[snafu::report]
fn main() -> Result<(), ConfigFileError> {
    read_config_file("bad-config.ini")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
This will print:

```
Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini
Caused by this error:
1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
Which shows the underlying errors, unlike [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html):

`Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini`… and is also more readable than the [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) output:

`Error: ConfigFileError { source: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }, path: "bad-config.ini" }`[§](https://docs.rs#next-steps)Next steps

Read the documentation for the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro to see all of the
capabilities, then read the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)for deeper understanding.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# kigumi_mod_base - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/kigumi-mod-base/1.0.0/kigumi_mod_base/

## Expand description

Base module: the foundational models other modules build on — currency, partner (contacts), and company. Root of the dependency graph (no dependencies of its own).

Multi-company: `res.company` is the unit of data isolation; transactional models carry a
`company_id` (added per model, e.g. sale.order). Partners are shared (no company_id) to avoid a
circular FK with res.company; company-specific contacts can be modelled later behind a deferred
FK. The active-company filtering rule lives in the security layer (Ctx.company + a record rule).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [seed](https://docs.rs/seed/index.html)
- Base reference data, run by the `register_seed!`seam at every migrate while`base`is installed: one default currency + company (multi-company needs a company to exist), a starter country set, and the read-only`res.groups`projection of every registered ACL/rule group. Every block is guarded by an exists-check — the DB is the authority, an operator change is never overwritten. Relocated verbatim from kigumi-cli so adopter binaries get it too.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IrAttachment](https://docs.rs/struct.IrAttachment.html)
- [ResCompany](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCompany.html)
- [ResCountry](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCountry.html)
- [ResCountry](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCountryState.html)- State
- [ResCurrency](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCurrency.html)
- [ResCurrency](https://docs.rs/struct.ResCurrencyRate.html)- Rate
- [ResGroups](https://docs.rs/struct.ResGroups.html)
- [ResPartner](https://docs.rs/struct.ResPartner.html)
- [ResUsers](https://docs.rs/struct.ResUsers.html)

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [ACLS](https://docs.rs/static.ACLS.html)
- Base ACLs: the everyday `user`group reads the foundational reference data and the group list; the user directory (`res.users`) is admin-only (read-only — account changes go through auth).`ir.attachment`generic CRUD is admin-only: end users reach files through the gated`/attachments`endpoints (which check host access and run elevated), never the raw model.
- [MANIFEST](https://docs.rs/static.MANIFEST.html)
- Module manifest. `base`depends on nothing and anchors the catalog.

# capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
struct FooImpl;
impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```

## Expand description

Headless HTTP layer (axum). Serves the integration surface from a model set: the OpenAPI spec, the model list, per-model UI contracts, and — when a database backend is provided — secured data endpoints that enforce the ACL + record-rule engine.

The server is agnostic of any module: a host wires its catalog in with
`kigumi_core::resolve_all_registered()` and its security policy, then calls [ router](https://docs.rs/fn.router.html) or

[. The core stays headless; this crate is optional.](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data.html)

`router_with_data`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_fingerprint.html)- fingerprint
- A cheap content hash of the DB-backed ACL/rule rows (owned data, no leak). The poll loop compares
it across ticks and only reloads the policy when it changes — so out-of-band edits (the `kigumi acl/rule`CLI, direct SQL) go live without paying the load_*_static string leak on every tick.
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_access.html)- access
- Recomputes the effective access policy — compiled-in baseline ∪ DB overrides — and swaps it into
the live snapshots, so a runtime ACL/rule change takes effect without a restart. On a DB load error
it KEEPS the prior good snapshot (it does not degrade to baseline-only — that would silently drop a
live restricting rule) and returns `false`, so the caller can retry on the next tick. Returns`true`only when both halves reloaded. NB it leaks the DB rows’ identifier strings (load_*_static), so the poll loop and the mutation endpoints guard it behind`access_fingerprint`
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_custom_fields.html)- custom_ - fields
- Reloads the live custom-field map from the registry (after an add, and at startup).
- [refresh_](https://docs.rs/fn.refresh_view_overrides.html)- view_ - overrides
- Reloads the live view-override map from `ir_ui_view`(after a change, and at startup). Owned data, so unlike the access policy this is leak-free and can run on every poll tick unconditionally.
- [router](https://docs.rs/fn.router.html)
- Metadata-only router: OpenAPI spec, model list, UI contracts. No database.
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data.html)- with_ - data
- Full router: metadata routes plus secured CRUD data endpoints. `auth_secret`is the HS256 secret used to verify the`Authorization: Bearer <token>`of each data request into a`Ctx`. No PDF rasterizer is configured (report`?format=pdf`answers 501); see`router_with_data_rasterized`
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data_dynamic.html)- with_ - data_ - dynamic
- Like `router_with_data`**live served catalog**:`installed`(a shared, mutable set of installed module names) gates which models are served, so installing/uninstalling a module via the`/api/modules/*`endpoints takes effect without restarting the process (the host passes the FULL linked catalog as`models`and keeps`installed`in sync with the DB). Used by`kigumi serve`.
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data_dynamic_rasterized.html)- with_ - data_ - dynamic_ - rasterized
- Like `router_with_data_dynamic``?format=pdf`(None → 501).
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_data_rasterized.html)- with_ - data_ - rasterized
- Like `router_with_data``?format=pdf`(None → those requests get 501).

- The effective access policy, swappable at runtime. Held as an `Arc`snapshot behind an`RwLock`: a request clones the current snapshot (cheap refcount bump) and reads it without holding the lock across`.await`, while the poll loop and the mutation endpoints replace the snapshot wholesale — so a DB-backed ACL/rule added via the CLI or the`/api/_acl``/api/_rule`endpoints takes effect with no restart, the same “declarative, no recompile” property as runtime custom fields.

# minhash_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/minhash-rs/0.3.3/minhash_rs/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#minhash-rs)MinHash-rs

A Rust implementation of MinHash trying to be parsimonious with memory.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-minhash)What is MinHash?

MinHash is a probabilistic data structure used to estimate the similarity between two sets. It is based on the observation that if we hash two sets of objects, the probability that the hashes agree is equal to the Jaccard similarity between the two sets.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-does-it-work)How does it work?

MinHash works by hashing the elements of a set and keeping track of the minimum hash value for each hash function. The probability that the minimum hash value of two sets is the same is equal to the Jaccard similarity between the two sets. By using multiple hash functions, we can estimate the Jaccard similarity between two sets by averaging the probability that the minimum hash value of the two sets is the same.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-this-crate)Using this crate

As usual, just add the following to your `Cargo.toml` file, although remember to check out the benchmark results below before going for MinHash over [HyperLogLog](https://github.com/LucaCappelletti94/hyperloglog-rs).

```
[dependencies]
minhash-rs = "0.3.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Build a sketch from each set and estimate their Jaccard similarity:

```
use std::collections::HashSet;
use minhash_rs::prelude::*;
let left: HashSet<u64> = (0..100).collect();
let right: HashSet<u64> = (50..150).collect();
// A MinHash over `u64` words with 256 permutations.
let left_sketch: MinHash<u64, 256> = left.iter().collect();
let right_sketch: MinHash<u64, 256> = right.iter().collect();
let estimate = left_sketch.estimate_jaccard_index(&right_sketch);
// The true Jaccard index here is 50 / 150 = 1/3.
let truth = 1.0 / 3.0;
assert!((estimate - truth).abs() < 0.1);
// Sketches can also be merged: `a | b` is the sketch of the union of the sets.
let union_sketch = left_sketch | right_sketch;
let union: HashSet<u64> = left.union(&right).copied().collect();
assert_eq!(union_sketch, union.iter().collect());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#locality-sensitive-hashing-lsh)Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)

Split a signature into bands to turn it into candidate keys for near-duplicate detection and similarity joins:

```
use minhash_rs::prelude::*;
let left: MinHash<u64, 128> = (0..100u64).collect();
let right: MinHash<u64, 128> = (0..100u64).collect();
let left_bands = left.band_hashes::<16>();
let right_bands = right.band_hashes::<16>();
assert!(left_bands.iter().zip(&right_bands).any(|(a, b)| a == b));
```
New benchmarks are under way.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [atomic](https://docs.rs/atomic/index.html)
- Hash generation and lock-free atomic insertion for MinHash sketches.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/from_iter/index.html)- iter
- `FromIterator`implementation that builds a MinHash from an iterator.
- [lsh](https://docs.rs/lsh/index.html)
- LSH banding for MinHash signatures.
- [maximal](https://docs.rs/maximal/index.html)
- Trait providing the maximal value of a word type.
- [minhash](https://docs.rs/minhash/index.html)
- Module providing the MinHash data structure.
- [minhash_](https://docs.rs/minhash_array/index.html)- array
- A fixed-size array of independent MinHash sketches.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports of the traits and types needed to use the crate.
- [primitive](https://docs.rs/primitive/index.html)
- Conversion of `u64`hash values into the narrower MinHash word types.

- Module proving implementations of the XorShift algorithm for several words.

# rqb-cli 0.1.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rqb-cli/0.1.3

# rqb-cli

`rqb-cli` introspects a Postgres database and emits a compact
`rqb::schema!` module for use with the `rqb` query builder.

The crate installs a binary named `rqb`.

## Install

Install from crates.io:

```
```
The package name is `rqb-cli`; the installed binary is `rqb`.

When working inside the rqb repository, run it through Cargo instead:

```
```
## Usage

Generate schema metadata from one Postgres schema:

```
```
`--database-url` also reads `DATABASE_URL`:

```
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/dbname \

```
Limit output to selected tables, views, or materialized views with repeated
`--table` flags:

```
```
Use `--config` when the generated schema needs project-owned type mappings:

```
```
Preview generated code without writing a file:

```
```
Fail CI when a checked-in schema file has drifted from the database:

```
```
Add `--report` when CI logs should show generation counts, raw-only columns,
and unused `type_map` entries:

```
```
Generated code is formatted with `rustfmt` by default. Pass `--no-rustfmt` when
`rustfmt` is not available on `PATH` or when you want raw generator output.
For drift checks, prefer the default formatted mode; `--check --no-rustfmt`
compares unformatted generator output against the file exactly as committed.

## Output

The output is one Rust file containing imports and a single `rqb::schema!`
invocation:

```
schema!
```
Known sqlx-supported Postgres types generate typed `Field<T>` constants.
Postgres enum types generate Rust enums with `sqlx::Type`, then enum columns
use those generated types:

```
schema!
```
Schema crates that include generated enums need a direct `sqlx` dependency with
the `derive` and `postgres` features enabled. Enum typing is scoped to the
generated Postgres schema; enum types from other schemas safely fall back to
raw-only metadata.

Unknown domains and extension types stay raw-only metadata, which can still be
used in server-owned SQL expressions through `*_META.expr()` or
`*_META.at("alias")`. This keeps extension columns available for server-owned
operators without pretending they have a portable Rust `Field<T>` mapping.

Map project-owned domains, extensions, or other PostgreSQL types in TOML:

```
[]
 = "crate::types::PgU256"
 = "ordered"        # none | equality | ordered | text; default none
 = "text"          # optional; omit to hide from SearchRequest
 = true           # also map bitcoin.uint256[] to Vec<crate::types::PgU256>
[]
 = "pgvector::Vector"
 = "none"
[]
 = [
  "public.vector_documents.search_index",
]
```
`rust` must be a qualified Rust type path and is emitted inline; the generator
does not add imports. The Rust type must implement the sqlx Postgres traits
required by the way it is used (`Type`, `Encode`, `Decode`, and array support
for `array = true`). rqb does not perform custom conversion.
`json` exposes only scalar columns to `SearchRequest`; generated array fields
stay JSON-hidden even when `array = true`.

When raw-only columns are generated, `rqb-cli` prints a stderr summary with the
relation, column, and Postgres type name. Treat that as a review queue for
project-specific enums, domains, ranges, and extension types that may deserve
manual raw helpers or future generator support.

`--deny-raw-only` turns that review queue into a CI failure unless every
raw-only column is listed in `[raw_only].allow` as `schema.relation.column`.
`--deny-unused-type-map` fails when a configured `[type_map."schema.type"]`
entry is not used by the selected `--schema` / `--table` scope. By default,
unused entries are warnings so stale config is visible without breaking local
generation.

The generator annotates schema facts that matter at the `sqlx::FromRow` or
write boundary:

```
// Nullable in Postgres metadata. Use Option<T> in row structs.
paid_at: timestamptz = ,
// Generated: stored. Do not include in INSERT assignments.
line_total_cents: int8 = i64,
// Identity: always. Do not include in INSERT assignments; use OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE to override.
invoice_no: int8 = i64,
// Identity: by default. Explicit INSERT values are allowed.
sequence_no: int8 = i64,
```
Materialized views are emitted as `view` entries with a `// Materialized view.`
comment. `rqb` queries them like normal read sources.

Non-deferrable primary-key and unique constraints generate a relation-local
`constraints` module:

```
schema!
insert
    .on_conflict_constraint
    .do_nothing;
```
## Boundaries

`rqb-cli` generates schema metadata, not application models. Row structs, API
DTOs, validation, redaction, and write commands stay in application code.

Nullable columns keep their normal `Field<T>` type in generated metadata. Use
`Option<T>` in `sqlx::FromRow` structs when the database column can return
`NULL`.

Foreign keys, check constraints, expression indexes, partial indexes, and
non-unique indexes are not introspected into the generated API. They remain
database constraints; runtime violations are mapped by `rqb::Error` when sqlx
returns them.

## Migrations

`rqb-cli` runs after migrations. It introspects the database that exists; it
does not generate migrations, diff schemas, or emit `ALTER TABLE`.

A typical CI check is:

-
Apply migrations with `sqlx::migrate!`,`sqlx migrate`, refinery, sqitch, psql, or your deployment system.
-
Verify the generated schema is current:

## Versioning

`rqb-cli` follows the same 0.x versioning as `rqb`. Before 1.0, minor versions
may change CLI flags or generated output shape when that improves the API.

---

# rqb - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqb/0.1.3/rqb/

## Expand description

SQL-first Postgres query builder for Rust services.

rqb is not an ORM. Application code owns SQL shape, rqb validates the typed
AST before rendering, and values are passed to Postgres as sqlx bind
arguments.
It is not a complete compile-time SQL type system: typed fields and bind
values make common service queries hard to mix up, but operator legality,
statement shape, and raw bind counts are runtime validation checks that fail
at `.build()?`.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-shape)Basic shape

Start with schema metadata. In applications this usually comes from
`rqb-cli` and the [ schema!](https://docs.rs/macro.schema.html) macro; small examples can write the macro
directly.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
rqb::schema! {
    table public.users {
        id: uuid = uuid::Uuid,
        email: text = String,
        active: bool = bool,
    }
}
let u = users::alias("u");
let query = rqb::select(&u)
    .column(u.id())
    .column(u.email())
    .filter(u.active().eq(true))
    .build()?;
```
`select(table())` projects known metadata fields, not `SELECT *`. Joined
fields and computed expressions stay explicit.

[§](https://docs.rs#imports)Imports

[ prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html) contains the builders, core AST types, schema support, execution
traits, and structured errors that normal service modules use. Broad SQL
helper names such as

`lower`, `left`, `array`, `row`, and `replace` are
available at the crate root for qualified calls, but are intentionally kept
out of [. The](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude`[alias is also kept qualified as](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)

`Result``rqb::Result` so application entry points can keep using their normal error
type. Import SQL helpers from [when a module wants short names.](https://docs.rs/dsl/index.html)

`dsl`[§](https://docs.rs#execution)Execution

Statements build parameterized Postgres SQL and execute through sqlx executors:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(sqlx::FromRow)]
struct UserRow {
    id: uuid::Uuid,
    email: String,
}
let users = rqb::select(users::table())
    .columns((users::ID, users::EMAIL))
    .filter(users::ACTIVE.eq(true))
    .fetch_all_as::<UserRow>(&pool)
    .await?;
```
Service functions can accept `&PgPool` by default. Reuse query-shape helper
functions when the same statement should run inside a transaction. Use
`impl PgExecutor<'_>` for small helpers that should execute directly from
both pool-backed code and transaction code. Pool-owned streaming helpers are
available for HTTP response streams where the returned stream must own the
built query.

[§](https://docs.rs#json-search-boundary)JSON search boundary

[ SearchRequest](https://docs.rs/struct.SearchRequest.html) lets client JSON control filters, sort, limit, and offset
only over fields exposed with

[. It cannot define tables, joins, raw SQL, CTEs, writes, subqueries, or projections. Use](https://docs.rs/struct.Meta.html#method.json)

`Meta::json`[to preserve tenant, permission, and other server-owned filters. When a request should own the whole search clause, start from a fresh](https://docs.rs/struct.Select.html#method.apply_search)

`Select::apply_search``select(...)` and call [there. LIKE and regex-style search operators require text-pattern field capability and reject very long client patterns before SQL is rendered; still set statement timeouts at HTTP or job boundaries for public search endpoints.](https://docs.rs/struct.Select.html#method.apply_search)

`Select::apply_search`[§](https://docs.rs#writes-and-raw-sql)Writes and raw SQL

Writes use field assignments or `#[derive(Insertable)]` /
`#[derive(Changeset)]`; there is no serde JSON write bridge. Raw SQL is still
server-owned and stays parameterized through [ raw](https://docs.rs/fn.raw.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/fn.raw_expr.html)

`raw_expr`[, and](https://docs.rs/fn.raw_predicate.html)

`raw_predicate`[. Raw placeholders are SQL-aware, but any raw fragment disables persistent prepared-statement caching for the whole built query.](https://docs.rs/fn.raw_source.html)

`raw_source`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [dsl](https://docs.rs/dsl/index.html)
- SQL expression and source helpers that are useful on demand but too broad for the prelude.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

# rqb_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqb-macros/0.1.3/rqb_macros/

## Expand description

Procedural macros used by the `rqb` facade crate.

Applications normally use these macros through `rqb::schema!`,
`#[derive(rqb::Insertable)]`, and `#[derive(rqb::Changeset)]`.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [schema](https://docs.rs/macro.schema.html)
- Generates compact rqb schema modules.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Changeset](https://docs.rs/derive.Changeset.html)
- Derives `rqb::Changeset`for patch DTOs.
- [Insertable](https://docs.rs/derive.Insertable.html)
- Derives `rqb::Insertable`for a DTO.

# shikumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shikumi/0.1.123/shikumi/

## Expand description

Shikumi (仕組み) — config discovery, hot-reload, and `ArcSwap` store
for Nix-managed desktop applications.

Extracted from [karakuri](https://github.com/pleme-io/karakuri)’s configuration
system, shikumi provides the shared infrastructure for desktop apps that need:

- **XDG config discovery**with env var overrides and format preference
- **Figment provider chains**(defaults → env vars → config file)
- **Lock-free concurrent reads**via- `ArcSwap`
- **Hot-reload**with symlink-aware file watching (for nix-darwin managed configs)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use shikumi::{ConfigDiscovery, ConfigStore, Format};
#[derive(Deserialize, Clone, Debug, Default)]
struct MyConfig {
    window_width: Option<u32>,
}
let path = ConfigDiscovery::new("myapp")
    .env_override("MYAPP_CONFIG")
    .formats(&[Format::Yaml, Format::Toml])
    .discover()
    .expect("config file not found");
let store = ConfigStore::<MyConfig>::load(&path, "MYAPP_")
    .expect("failed to load config");
let config = store.get();
println!("width: {:?}", config.window_width);
```

# snafu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snafu/latest/snafu/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#snafu)SNAFU

SNAFU is a library to easily generate errors and add information to underlying errors, especially when the same underlying error type can occur in different contexts.

For detailed information, please see the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro and the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- [Turnkey errors based on strings](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)
- [Custom error types](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)- Including a conversion path from turnkey errors

- [Backtraces](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- Extension traits for
- [Error reporting](https://docs.rs#reporting)
- Suitable for libraries and applications
- `no_std`compatibility
- Generic types and lifetimes

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

If you want to report errors without hassle, start with the
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) type and the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)

`whatever!````
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Whatever> {
    if id < 10 {
        whatever!("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
You can also use it to wrap any other error:

```
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Whatever> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path)
        .with_whatever_context(|_| format!("Could not read file {path}"))
}
```
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) allows for a short message and tracks a

[for every error:](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)

`Backtrace````
use snafu::{prelude::*, ErrorCompat, Whatever};
if let Err(e) = returns_an_error() {
    eprintln!("An error occurred: {e}");
    if let Some(bt) = ErrorCompat::backtrace(&e) {
        eprintln!("{bt}");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-error-types)Custom error types

Many projects will hit limitations of the `Whatever` type. When
that occurs, it’s time to create your own error type by deriving
[ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)!

[§](https://docs.rs#struct-style)Struct style

SNAFU will read your error struct definition and create a *context
selector* type (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this example). These
context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html) macro to provide
ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
struct InvalidIdError {
    id: u16,
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), InvalidIdError> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to your error, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#enum-style)Enum style

While error structs are good for constrained cases, they don’t allow for reporting multiple possible kinds of errors at one time. Error enums solve that problem.

SNAFU will read your error enum definition and create a *context
selector* type for each variant (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this
example). These context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
macro to provide ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to a variant, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
    ConfigFile {
        source: std::io::Error,
        path: String,
    },
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Error> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
You can combine the power of the [ whatever!](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html) macro with an
enum error type. This is great if you started out with

[and are moving to a custom error type:](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)

`Whatever````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
    #[snafu(whatever, display("{message}"))]
    Whatever {
        message: String,
        #[snafu(source(from(Box<dyn std::error::Error>, Some)))]
        source: Option<Box<dyn std::error::Error>>,
    },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    whatever!("Just kidding... this function always fails!");
    Ok(())
}
```
You may wish to make the type `Send` and/or `Sync`, allowing
your error type to be used in multithreaded programs, by changing
`dyn std::error::Error` to `dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#reporting)Reporting

Printing an error via [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)
will only show the top-level error message without the underlying sources.
For an extended error report,
SNAFU offers a user-friendly error output mechanism.
It prints the main error and all underlying errors in the chain,
from the most recent to the oldest,
plus the

[backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)if applicable. This is done by using the

[procedural macro or the](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)

`report`[type directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)

`Report````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not load configuration file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
#[snafu::report]
fn main() -> Result<(), ConfigFileError> {
    read_config_file("bad-config.ini")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
This will print:

```
Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini
Caused by this error:
1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
Which shows the underlying errors, unlike [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html):

`Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini`… and is also more readable than the [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) output:

`Error: ConfigFileError { source: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }, path: "bad-config.ini" }`[§](https://docs.rs#next-steps)Next steps

Read the documentation for the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro to see all of the
capabilities, then read the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)for deeper understanding.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Ensure a condition is true. If it is not, return from the function with an error.
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure_whatever.html)- whatever - `alloc`
- Ensure a condition is true. If it is not, return a stringly-typed error message.
- [location](https://docs.rs/macro.location.html)
- Constructs a `Location`
- [whatever](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)- `alloc`
- Instantiate and return a stringly-typed error message.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- A captured OS thread stack backtrace.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainCompat.html)- Compat
- An iterator over an Error and its sources.
- [Cleaned](https://docs.rs/struct.CleanedErrorText.html)- Error - Text - `alloc`
- An iterator over an Error and its sources that removes duplicated text from the error display strings.
- [None](https://docs.rs/struct.NoneError.html)- Error
- A temporary error type used when converting an `Option``Result`
- [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)
- Opinionated solution to format an error in a user-friendly
way. Useful as the return type from `main`and test functions.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)- `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.WhateverLocal.html)- Local - `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling when the error does not need to cross a thread boundary.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsBacktrace](https://docs.rs/trait.AsBacktrace.html)
- View a backtrace-like value as an optional backtrace.
- [AsError](https://docs.rs/trait.AsErrorSource.html)- Source
- Converts the receiver into an `Error``Error::source`
- [Error](https://docs.rs/trait.ErrorCompat.html)- Compat
- Backports changes to the `Error`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromString.html)- String - `alloc`
- Takes a string message and builds the corresponding error.
- [Generate](https://docs.rs/trait.GenerateImplicitData.html)- Implicit - Data
- Construct data to be included as part of an error. The data must require no arguments to be created.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoError.html)- Error
- Combines an underlying error with additional information about the error.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionExt.html)- Ext
- Additions to `Option`
- [Result](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html)- Ext
- Additions to `Result`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Location](https://docs.rs/type.Location.html)
- The source code location where the error was reported.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [report](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)
- Adapts a function to provide user-friendly error output for `main`functions and tests.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)
- The `Snafu`macro is the entrypoint to defining your own error types. It is designed to require little configuration for the recommended and typical usecases while still offering flexibility for unique situations.

# backtrace 0.3.76 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/backtrace/^0.3.0

# backtrace-rs

A library for acquiring backtraces at runtime for Rust. This library aims to enhance the support of the standard library by providing a programmatic interface to work with, but it also supports simply easily printing the current backtrace like libstd's panics.

## Install

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
## Usage

To simply capture a backtrace and defer dealing with it until a later time,
you can use the top-level `Backtrace` type.

```
use Backtrace;
```
If, however, you'd like more raw access to the actual tracing functionality, you
can use the `trace` and `resolve` functions directly.

```
```
# Supported Rust Versions

The `backtrace` crate is a core component of the standard library, and must
at times keep up with the evolution of various platforms in order to serve
the standard library's needs. This often means using recent libraries
that provide unwinding and symbolication for various platforms.
Thus `backtrace` is likely to use recent Rust features or depend on a library
which itself uses them. Its minimum supported Rust version, by policy, is
within a few versions of current stable, approximately "stable - 2".

This policy takes precedence over versions written anywhere else in this repo.

documentation](https://docs.rs/snafu) and the [user's guide](https://docs.rs/snafu/*/snafu/guide/index.html) for a full
description.

# snafu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snafu

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#snafu)SNAFU

SNAFU is a library to easily generate errors and add information to underlying errors, especially when the same underlying error type can occur in different contexts.

For detailed information, please see the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro and the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- [Turnkey errors based on strings](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)
- [Custom error types](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)- Including a conversion path from turnkey errors

- [Backtraces](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- Extension traits for
- [Error reporting](https://docs.rs#reporting)
- Suitable for libraries and applications
- `no_std`compatibility
- Generic types and lifetimes

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

If you want to report errors without hassle, start with the
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) type and the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)

`whatever!````
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Whatever> {
    if id < 10 {
        whatever!("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
You can also use it to wrap any other error:

```
use snafu::{prelude::*, Whatever};
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Whatever> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path)
        .with_whatever_context(|_| format!("Could not read file {path}"))
}
```
[ Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html) allows for a short message and tracks a

[for every error:](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)

`Backtrace````
use snafu::{prelude::*, ErrorCompat, Whatever};
if let Err(e) = returns_an_error() {
    eprintln!("An error occurred: {e}");
    if let Some(bt) = ErrorCompat::backtrace(&e) {
        eprintln!("{bt}");
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-error-types)Custom error types

Many projects will hit limitations of the `Whatever` type. When
that occurs, it’s time to create your own error type by deriving
[ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)!

[§](https://docs.rs#struct-style)Struct style

SNAFU will read your error struct definition and create a *context
selector* type (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this example). These
context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html) macro to provide
ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
struct InvalidIdError {
    id: u16,
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), InvalidIdError> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to your error, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#enum-style)Enum style

While error structs are good for constrained cases, they don’t allow for reporting multiple possible kinds of errors at one time. Error enums solve that problem.

SNAFU will read your error enum definition and create a *context
selector* type for each variant (called `InvalidIdSnafu` in this
example). These context selectors are used with the [ ensure!](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
macro to provide ergonomic error creation:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    Ok(())
}
```
If you add a `source` field to a variant, you can then wrap an
underlying error using the [ context](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html#tymethod.context)
extension method:

```
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("Could not read file {path}"))]
    ConfigFile {
        source: std::io::Error,
        path: String,
    },
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, Error> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
```
You can combine the power of the [ whatever!](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html) macro with an
enum error type. This is great if you started out with

[and are moving to a custom error type:](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)

`Whatever````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
enum Error {
    #[snafu(display("ID may not be less than 10, but it was {id}"))]
    InvalidId { id: u16 },
    #[snafu(whatever, display("{message}"))]
    Whatever {
        message: String,
        #[snafu(source(from(Box<dyn std::error::Error>, Some)))]
        source: Option<Box<dyn std::error::Error>>,
    },
}
fn is_valid_id(id: u16) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ensure!(id >= 10, InvalidIdSnafu { id });
    whatever!("Just kidding... this function always fails!");
    Ok(())
}
```
You may wish to make the type `Send` and/or `Sync`, allowing
your error type to be used in multithreaded programs, by changing
`dyn std::error::Error` to `dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync`.

[§](https://docs.rs#reporting)Reporting

Printing an error via [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)
will only show the top-level error message without the underlying sources.
For an extended error report,
SNAFU offers a user-friendly error output mechanism.
It prints the main error and all underlying errors in the chain,
from the most recent to the oldest,
plus the

[backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)if applicable. This is done by using the

[procedural macro or the](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)

`report`[type directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)

`Report````
use snafu::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, Snafu)]
#[snafu(display("Could not load configuration file {path}"))]
struct ConfigFileError {
    source: std::io::Error,
    path: String,
}
fn read_config_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, ConfigFileError> {
    std::fs::read_to_string(path).context(ConfigFileSnafu { path })
}
#[snafu::report]
fn main() -> Result<(), ConfigFileError> {
    read_config_file("bad-config.ini")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
This will print:

```
Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini
Caused by this error:
1: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
Which shows the underlying errors, unlike [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html):

`Error: Could not load configuration file bad-config.ini`… and is also more readable than the [ Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) output:

`Error: ConfigFileError { source: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }, path: "bad-config.ini" }`[§](https://docs.rs#next-steps)Next steps

Read the documentation for the [ Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html) macro to see all of the
capabilities, then read the

[user’s guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)for deeper understanding.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [futures](https://docs.rs/futures/index.html)- `futures`
- Additions to the `TryFuture``TryStream`
- [guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html)- `guide`
- SNAFU user’s guide
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Traits and macros used by most projects. Add `use snafu::prelude::*`to your code to quickly get started with SNAFU.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Ensure a condition is true. If it is not, return from the function with an error.
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure_whatever.html)- whatever - `alloc`
- Ensure a condition is true. If it is not, return a stringly-typed error message.
- [location](https://docs.rs/macro.location.html)
- Constructs a `Location`
- [whatever](https://docs.rs/macro.whatever.html)- `alloc`
- Instantiate and return a stringly-typed error message.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Backtrace](https://docs.rs/struct.Backtrace.html)
- A captured OS thread stack backtrace.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainCompat.html)- Compat
- An iterator over an Error and its sources.
- [Cleaned](https://docs.rs/struct.CleanedErrorText.html)- Error - Text - `alloc`
- An iterator over an Error and its sources that removes duplicated text from the error display strings.
- [None](https://docs.rs/struct.NoneError.html)- Error
- A temporary error type used when converting an `Option``Result`
- [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)
- Opinionated solution to format an error in a user-friendly
way. Useful as the return type from `main`and test functions.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.Whatever.html)- `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling.
- [Whatever](https://docs.rs/struct.WhateverLocal.html)- Local - `alloc`
- A basic error type that you can use as a first step to better error handling when the error does not need to cross a thread boundary.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsBacktrace](https://docs.rs/trait.AsBacktrace.html)
- View a backtrace-like value as an optional backtrace.
- [AsError](https://docs.rs/trait.AsErrorSource.html)- Source
- Converts the receiver into an `Error``Error::source`
- [Error](https://docs.rs/trait.ErrorCompat.html)- Compat
- Backports changes to the `Error`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromString.html)- String - `alloc`
- Takes a string message and builds the corresponding error.
- [Generate](https://docs.rs/trait.GenerateImplicitData.html)- Implicit - Data
- Construct data to be included as part of an error. The data must require no arguments to be created.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoError.html)- Error
- Combines an underlying error with additional information about the error.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionExt.html)- Ext
- Additions to `Option`
- [Result](https://docs.rs/trait.ResultExt.html)- Ext
- Additions to `Result`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Location](https://docs.rs/type.Location.html)
- The source code location where the error was reported.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [report](https://docs.rs/attr.report.html)
- Adapts a function to provide user-friendly error output for `main`functions and tests.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Snafu](https://docs.rs/derive.Snafu.html)
- The `Snafu`macro is the entrypoint to defining your own error types. It is designed to require little configuration for the recommended and typical usecases while still offering flexibility for unique situations.

These are the policies for upholding our community's standards of
conduct. If you feel that a thread needs moderation, please notify
[@shepmaster][].
1.
2.
3.

We strive to go the extra step to look out for each other. Don't just
aim to be technically unimpeachable, try to be your best self. In
particular, avoid flirting with offensive or sensitive issues,
particularly if they're off-topic; this all too often leads to
unnecessary fights, hurt feelings, and damaged trust; worse, it can
drive people away from the community entirely.
If someone takes issue with something you said or did, resist the urge
to be defensive. Just stop doing what it was they complained about and
apologize. Even if you feel you were misinterpreted or unfairly
accused, chances are good there was something you could've
communicated better — remember that it's your responsibility to make
your fellow humans comfortable. Everyone wants to get along and we
are all here first and foremost because we want to talk about cool
technology. You will find that people will be eager to assume good
intent and forgive as long as you earn their trust.

# backtrace 0.3.76 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/backtrace/0.3.76

# backtrace-rs

A library for acquiring backtraces at runtime for Rust. This library aims to enhance the support of the standard library by providing a programmatic interface to work with, but it also supports simply easily printing the current backtrace like libstd's panics.

## Install

```
[]
 = "0.3"
```
## Usage

To simply capture a backtrace and defer dealing with it until a later time,
you can use the top-level `Backtrace` type.

```
use Backtrace;
```
If, however, you'd like more raw access to the actual tracing functionality, you
can use the `trace` and `resolve` functions directly.

```
```
# Supported Rust Versions

The `backtrace` crate is a core component of the standard library, and must
at times keep up with the evolution of various platforms in order to serve
the standard library's needs. This often means using recent libraries
that provide unwinding and symbolication for various platforms.
Thus `backtrace` is likely to use recent Rust features or depend on a library
which itself uses them. Its minimum supported Rust version, by policy, is
within a few versions of current stable, approximately "stable - 2".

This policy takes precedence over versions written anywhere else in this repo.

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1.0/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

---

# cpp_demangle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpp_demangle/^0.5.0/

## Expand description

This crate can parse a C++ “mangled” linker symbol name into a Rust value
describing what the name refers to: a variable, a function, a virtual table,
etc. The description type implements functions such as `demangle()`,
producing human-readable text describing the mangled name. Debuggers and
profilers can use this crate to provide more meaningful output.

C++ requires the compiler to choose names for linker symbols consistently
across compilation units, so that two compilation units that have seen the
same declarations can pair up definitions in one unit with references in
another.  Almost all platforms other than Microsoft Windows follow the
[Itanium C++ ABI](https://itanium-cxx-abi.github.io/cxx-abi/abi.html#mangling)’s rules for this.

For example, suppose a C++ compilation unit has the definition:

```
namespace space {
  int foo(int x, int y) { return x+y; }
}
```
The Itanium C++ ABI specifies that the linker symbol for that function must
be named `_ZN5space3fooEii`. This crate can parse that name into a Rust
value representing its structure. That Rust value can be `demangle()`d to the
string `space::foo(int, int)`, which is more meaningful to the C++
developer.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- Abstract syntax tree types for mangled symbols.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Custom `Error`and`Result`types for the`cpp_demangle`crate.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Demangle](https://docs.rs/struct.DemangleOptions.html)- Options
- Options to control the demangling process.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseOptions.html)- Options
- Options to control the parsing process.
- [Symbol](https://docs.rs/struct.Symbol.html)
- A mangled symbol that has been parsed into an AST.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Demangle](https://docs.rs/enum.DemangleNodeType.html)- Node - Type
- The type of a demangled AST node. This is only partial, not all nodes are represented.
